definition: The Endangered Species Act (ESA), codified at 16 U.S.C. § 1531 et seq., is a federal law enacted to prevent species from becoming extinct due to unchecked economic development. It aims to protect both endangered and threatened species and “the ecosystems on which endangered species and threatened species depend.” Listing The ESA applies only to species listed as “endangered” or “threatened.” A species may be listed in two ways: Directly by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) or the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), including the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), through a candidate assessment program. By petition from an individual or organization requesting the FWS or NMFS to list the species. To be listed, a species must meet at least one of five criteria under §4(a)(1):  Present or threatened destruction, modification, or curtailment of its habitat or range  Overutilization for commercial, recreational, scientific, or educational purposes  Disease or predation  Inadequacy of existing regulatory mechanisms  Other natural or manmade factors affecting its continued existence Candidate species are prioritized, with “emergency listing” reserved for those facing significant risk to their survival. Federal Agency Actions Under §7(a)(2), federal agencies may not authorize, fund, or carry out any action likely to jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or damage their critical habitat. The Supreme Court affirmed in TVA v. Hill, 437 U.S. 153 (1978), that the ESA requires species protection regardless of cost. In that case, the Court enjoined the operation of a nearly completed dam to protect the snail darter fish. Although this provision does not directly regulate private landowners, many major projects, such as logging, mining, or development, require federal permits and are therefore subject to ESA compliance. Private Actions Section 9(a)(1) prohibits any person, public or private, from “taking” an endangered species of fish or wildlife. “Take” includes actions such as harassing, harming, pursuing, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capturing, or collecting.
